# LLMs are compressors. So I chatted with gzip
URL: https://edoardodusi.com/blog/2026/gzip-chat.html
Date: 2026-11-16
Reading time: 16 min

I had a conversation with a chatbot this morning:

```text
› who is edo?
● a senior developer advocate at aws, turning hard tech into talks developers remember.

› what talk did edo give at oredev?
● bundlers: a deep dive into modern javascript build tools, nov 2025; honey, i shrunk
  the bits: how modern http compression works, nov 2025.

› what is the capital of italy?
● i don't know. that question surprises me too much.
```

First answer is correct, second is correct, third is an honest refusal. Nothing special for a chatbot, right? Except that this one has no neural network, no GPU and no weights. Every letter of every answer was chosen by **gzip** (except the refusal, I'll get to that). At each step it tries every possible next letter and keeps the one that compresses smallest. The same DEFLATE algorithm that compresses the HTTP responses of the page you're reading.

![The gzip chat page in dark mode: a header that says model gzip, parameters 0, and four questions with their answers, the last one a refusal](/img/posts/gzip-chat/chat-trained.png)

You can [try it yourself](https://d2v8qi14yayt65.cloudfront.net): click a question, then switch to *untrained* to see what gzip writes with no data. But to understand why this apparently silly experiment (not my original idea, BTW) works at all, we have to talk about what *compressing* really means.

What's in this article:

- why compressing and predicting are the same job
- what gzip "predicts", and how to make it write
- what it took to turn it into a chat, and where it breaks
- why, in the end, the code around the model does most of the work.

Oh, about the POC itself, I built it with [Kiro Crew](https://github.com/kirodotdev/KiroCrew), an AI agent that wrote the code while I steered the design, so when I say "we" below, that's the two of us.

## LLMs are compressors

In 2023 a team at **Google DeepMind** published a paper whose title is also its thesis: [Language Modeling Is Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.10668). They took 1 GB of English Wikipedia and compressed it with classic tools and with language models.

*gzip*, given the whole file at once, shrinks it to 32.3% of its size. But a language model can only read a few kilobytes at a time, so for a like-for-like test they also cut the file into 2 KB pieces, and on those pieces gzip only gets to 48.1% (each piece starts with no context, so gzip has less to copy).

Chinchilla, a 70 billion parameter model, on the same 2 KB pieces, compressed the same file to **8.3%** of its size. About *six times better than gzip*.

To be fair, if you count the model itself as part of the compressed file (the receiver needs it to decompress), Chinchilla's rate becomes 14,008%. gzip's whole program is a few kilobytes. That's why LLMs are impractical compressors, at least for a 1 GB file.

Then in section 3.4, the paper argues that if a predictor can be used as a compressor, then a compressor can also be used as a predictor...so they made gzip write text. After reading a page of Wikipedia, this is what it wrote:

```text
(0k5Ezatme,isbebmvcsouL(nxscbiife peu7vevwt parr,iswfommeeaa are nombban hm
```

It's gibberish, and the authors explain why: their setup only looks one step ahead, which is biased for gzip, and "it's likely that looking multiple steps ahead would improve the results". That wasn't the purpose of their paper, so they stopped there.

But it's the purpose of my article, so I tried.

If you want the long, friendly version of the theory, Annie Sexton's [Compression is prediction](https://ngrok.com/blog/compression-is-prediction) on the ngrok blog is a great read. This is the short version.

## Why compressing means predicting

Think about your phone keyboard. I want to write "see you tomorrow", and it suggests "see", "you" and "tomorrow", one tap each: fourteen letters, three taps. Now give me a phone whose keyboard learned Italian, and while I type "home" it suggests "ho", "hai", "hanno". All wrong, so I type every letter by hand. The guesser changed, so the message became more expensive.

Now imagine the person receiving my message has exactly the same keyboard. When the guess is right, I don't send the word at all, I send "yes, take your guess". Only when the guess is wrong do I need to send the correction. **You only send what the receiver can't guess.** That's compression! Every compressor works like this: the same guesser is on both sides, and only the misses must travel.

This isn't a metaphor I made up.

In 1951 Claude Shannon ran exactly this game in [Prediction and Entropy of Printed English](https://archive.org/details/bstj30-1-50). He asked a person to guess a phrase letter by letter, and wrote a dash every time they got it right on the first try:

```text
THE ROOM WAS NOT VERY LIGHT A SMALL OBLONG
----ROO------NOT-V-----I------SM----OBL---
```

On the full passage (where spaces count as letters too), 89 letters out of 129 were dashes. Shannon's point was that the second line contains the same information as the first. If you have an *identical twin* of the person who guessed, the twin can rebuild the sentence from the dashes alone.

The price of a letter is its **surprise**. A guess the model is sure about costs almost nothing, a surprise is expensive. In bits, a symbol you expected with probability p costs `-log2(p)`: a coin flip is 1 bit, a sure thing is 0. With this game Shannon estimated that ordinary English carries something like one bit per letter, instead of the 4.7 bits of a random letter.

So a compressor is exactly as good as its guesses. Take one sentence and three different guessers:

| "To be or not to be, that is the question." | Size |
| --- | --- |
| Plain text, 41 bytes | 328 bits |
| DEFLATE, the algorithm inside gzip | 320 bits |
| A small LLM (Qwen2.5-0.5B, about 1 GB of weights) on both sides | 30 bits |

The LLM has read Shakespeare, so after "to be" almost nothing is a surprise. gzip has read nothing, so it saves one byte (BTW a `.gz` file, with its 18 bytes of header, ends up bigger than the text).

This is a demo I ran on stage. For every token, the model lists its guesses, and the sender only notes where the real token was in that list: rank 1 means the first guess was right. Only those ranks travel, and the receiver runs the same model, picks the guess at each rank, and rebuilds the sentence byte for byte. Ranks are just the easy way to see it: the 30 bits in the table is what a real coder (arithmetic coding) pays with the model's probabilities, about `-log2(p)` per token, so a confident guess costs a fraction of a bit.

![A terminal running Qwen2.5-0.5B on "To be or not to be, that is the question.": each token gets a rank and a cost in bits, "To", "be" and "or" are expensive, almost everything after is rank 1 and nearly free, the ranks 40 4 97 1 1 1 2 1 1 1 1 2 travel, and the receiver rebuilds the sentence byte for byte](/img/posts/gzip-chat/qwen-rank.gif)

"To", "be" and "or" cost 24 of the 30 bits, because until then the model doesn't know it's Shakespeare. Everything after is a first guess and almost free. (The "gzip 456 bits" on screen is the `.gz` file made by Python, header included. Python's zlib gets the stream to 39 bytes, one less than Node's.) Let's look at what gzip guesses with.

## gzip's model is its own past

DEFLATE is two algorithms stacked. The first, **LZ77**, replaces repeated text with a pointer: "copy 12 bytes from 40 bytes back". The second, Huffman coding, gives shorter codes to the things that show up more often. What matters here is the first one: text that repeats is cheap, text that's new is expensive.

Oh, and gzip can only look 32 KB back, that's its whole context window.

So gzip predicts exactly one thing: that the text will repeat what it has already seen. On a long Wikipedia dump that's a decent bet, because a lot of patterns repeat. On one line of Shakespeare there's nothing to copy, so the bet loses.

## Making gzip write

If gzip's guess is "whatever compresses best", we can ask it to write with a simple loop. Take the text so far, add every possible next character, compress each version, and keep the one that came out smallest. That's the character gzip "expected". Then repeat. In an LLM this is called *greedy decoding*, at temperature 0.

We never touch gzip's code, the only question we ask it is "how many bytes is this?"

```ts
// src/engine.ts (simplified)
import zlib from 'node:zlib';

const ALPHABET = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz .,':;0123456789\n";

// The only thing we ever ask gzip
const size = (text: string, dictionary?: Buffer) =>
  zlib.deflateRawSync(text, { level: 9, dictionary }).length;

// The next character gzip "expects": the one that keeps the output smallest
function nextChar(text: string, dictionary?: Buffer): string {
  let best = ALPHABET[0];
  let bestSize = Infinity;
  for (const c of ALPHABET) {
    const s = size(text + c, dictionary);
    if (s < bestSize) [best, bestSize] = [c, s];
  }
  return best;
}
```

That's the naive version, and if you run it on the sentence about the cat below, it writes "mat" and then "aaaa" forever. The talk version of this demo did the same at first. The reason is that sizes come in whole bytes, so a preference of a few bits disappears, all 43 characters tie, and the first one in the alphabet wins. The fix has two parts, and only ever uses sizes. When characters tie, the real engine continues each one for 4 more characters and keeps the one whose continuation compresses best. This is the paper's "looking multiple steps ahead". To compare those continuations it has to see differences smaller than a byte. DEFLATE writes bits but rounds the output up to whole bytes, so a difference of a few bits usually doesn't show. Adding filler of different lengths moves where that rounding falls, so the engine compresses each continuation 16 times with a different filler, and the sum shows the small differences.

This is untrained gzip, with no data and nothing but the text you type:

![The untrained mode of gzip chat: the cat sentence continued by copying, the Hamlet line looping on itself, and xyz turning into a row of a](/img/posts/gzip-chat/chat-untrained.png)

- "the cat sat on the mat. the dog sat on the log. the cat sat on the " becomes "**mat. the dog sat on the log. the cat sat**". It copies.
- "to be or not to be, that is the " becomes "**or not to be, that is the or not to be**". It loops, because the cheapest thing to write is a copy of what it just wrote.
- "xyz" becomes "**aaaaaaaa**". Nothing to copy, no preference.

So gzip can write, but only what it has already read. Let's give it something to read!

## Training gzip

zlib has a feature called the **preset dictionary**: text that gzip reads before it starts compressing, as if it had already seen it. (Strictly speaking it's a DEFLATE feature: the `.gz` file format has no room for a dictionary, so the code calls raw DEFLATE.) Whatever is in the dictionary becomes cheap to copy. That's gzip's "training data", and like its memory, it's capped at 32 KB.

I first did this for a talk. I gave gzip the talk's own notes plus a few questions and answers, and let the room ask it things. Highlight of the talk, if you ask me.

The trick that turns completion into a chat is the format. If the dictionary is full of lines like `q: who is edo? a: a senior developer advocate...`, and I give gzip `q: <your question>? a:`, the cheapest continuation is an answer copied from a line that looks like yours. That's a chat template, the same trick as giving a base LLM a few example questions and answers in its prompt.

It also hallucinates, with zero parameters. Ask it something it doesn't know, and it confidently copies the answer of whatever line looks closest.

## RAG, with gzip only

In the demo, the knowledge comes from my website: 477 questions sharing 104 answers, 26 KB. The answers are sentences from the site, lightly shortened (apart from a few about the chat itself), and a script turns the lists of talks and articles into pairs. The questions, and the many ways to word each one, were written by Kiro Crew. So yes, an LLM wrote gzip's training data.

To answer, gzip first has to find the right pair. The idea is old and lovely: two texts that share a lot cost little more to compress together than apart. Compare one question with two stored ones:

| "which city is edo in?" with... | Alone | Together | Extra bytes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| "which city does edo live in?" | 26 + 33 | 40 | **7** |
| "what is the schema tax?" | 26 + 28 | 48 | **20** |

The first pair shares "which city ... edo ... in?", so gzip copies those words and adding the question costs almost nothing. Turn that into a number between 0 and 1 (the size together, minus the smaller one alone, divided by the bigger one) and you get the [normalized compression distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalized_compression_distance): close to 0 means the same text, close to 1 means nothing in common.

That number also gives gzip a way to say no. If even the closest stored question is too far away (a distance above 0.45), it doesn't copy anything. It answers "i don't know. that question surprises me too much". If your question is too surprising, gzip has nothing to copy, and my code says so with a sentence I wrote.

Then it writes, with only the closest pairs as its dictionary. How many? We measured it on the 15 test questions that have an answer, with the refusal turned off, and fewer pairs work better:

| What gzip reads while writing | Right answers (of 15) |
| --- | --- |
| the closest pair | 10 |
| **the 3 closest pairs** | **11** |
| the 10 closest | 8 |
| the 30 closest | 6 |
| all 477, closest last | 5 |
| all 477, no retrieval | 3 |

(Written out as pairs, all 477 take 54 KB, so in the last two rows gzip only sees the last 32 KB.)

Every extra pair is one more place to copy from by mistake. A nice side effect: retrieval also removes the 32 KB limit, because gzip only ever reads a few hundred bytes per answer.

How good is it? We scored it on 20 questions written before scoring and never added to the data. It answered 10 of the 15 it had an answer for (the refusal costs one right answer, the MCP one), and refused all 5 it had no answer for, like the president of Italy or my email address. It's a demo number, not a benchmark, before you quote it.

The failures are more interesting than the score.

![gzip chat answering "does edo have kids?" correctly, and "does edo have offspring?" with the description of the podcast](/img/posts/gzip-chat/chat-bytes-not-meaning.png)

"does edo have kids?" works, because someone wrote "kids" down. To gzip, "does edo have offspring?" is exactly as far from "does edo have a podcast?" as from "does edo have kids?" (eight stored questions tie). The podcast one comes first in the file, so I get my podcast described to me. gzip matches **bytes**, not **meaning**.

The second kind is subtler: even when retrieval finds the right question, gzip can copy the wrong answer, when two answers cost exactly the same bytes and the alphabet breaks the tie.

## How it runs

gzip chat is one Node.js HTTP server with no dependencies, deployed as an [AWS Lambda Web Function](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/web-functions.html) behind Amazon CloudFront.

![The browser calls Amazon CloudFront, which caches answers. The first time a question is asked, CloudFront forwards it, signed with SigV4, to the gzip-chat Lambda Web Function in eu-west-1, which holds zlib and 26 KB of Q&A](/img/posts/gzip-chat/architecture.png)

gzip is deterministic: the same question always gets the same answer. So CloudFront caches every answer for a day (the question travels in the URL, so it's the cache key), and only the first person to ask something new wakes the function. A new answer takes from a few milliseconds to under two seconds of CPU, and the function scales to zero when nobody is asking.

One confession: the letter-by-letter typing on the page is theatre. The server sends the whole answer at once, and the page animates it so you can watch it like a chat. In the next version I will add some "discombobulating..." somewhere.

The code is on [GitHub](https://github.com/edodusi/gzip-chat), with the eval (`npm run eval`), a one-command deploy and a teardown script.

## So, is gzip an LLM?

NO!

gzip makes almost every choice: every letter of an answer, which stored question is closest, when an answer ends. I wrote the rules and the data: the knowledge file, the `q: ... a:` template, the 0.45 cutoff, the 3 pairs, the refusal sentence. When it answers right, it has almost always copied a stored answer word for word. It's a search engine with a copy machine attached. A RAG in miniature.

In my opinion that's still a good way to understand how an LLM chatbot works, just in reverse. An LLM chatbot has the same parts: a model that predicts the next token, and around it the chat template, the retrieval, the system prompt and the stop rules, code that people wrote. We call this the **harness**. In gzip chat the harness does almost all the work, because the model can only copy.

An LLM learned from billions of sentences that "kids" and "offspring" show up in the same places, so it knows they mean the same thing, and nobody has to write down every wording or decide for it when to say "i don't know". gzip only remembers bytes, so every way to say something has to be written down for it. That's what all those parameters buy you: a thin harness. And it's why an LLM had to write gzip's "training data".

Both of them only send you what you couldn't guess. The better the guesser, the less the rest of the system has to do.

---

# Is stateless MCP just REST? I ran 180 tests to find out
URL: https://edoardodusi.com/blog/2026/mcp-vs-rest-measured.html
Date: 2026-10-26
Reading time: 14 min

> **Update, 2026-11-03:** an earlier version of this post said REST reads its contract only once. That's wrong for this harness: Converse is stateless, so the REST contract is re-sent on every call, exactly like the MCP schemas. A reader, [izgorodin](https://dev.to/izgorodin/comment/3jfi4), spotted it and proposed a control experiment. I ran it, and the results are in the new section after Result 4. The 35% gap is real, but it comes from how dense the description is, not from where it sits.

In July 2026 the Model Context Protocol [dropped sessions](https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2026-07-28/). The handshake is gone, the `Mcp-Session-Id` header is gone, and every request now stands on its own. Within a week the internet did what the internet does, compressing that change into a slogan: MCP is dead, REST won, it was always just REST with extra steps.

In the [2026-07-28 MCP spec](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/changelog), `tools/list` no longer varies per connection, and a server that needs cross-call state now mints an explicit handle and passes it back as an ordinary tool argument. In other words, a stateless MCP server is now a list of tool names with JSON schemas, presented to the model, which emits a tool call that the host dispatches.

Say that out loud and the REST comparison writes itself. Maybe even the slogan. A REST API is *also* stateless HTTP.

I always loved that "computer scientist" has the word **scientist** in it, so I want proof and measurements, even for silly slogans. I found no measurement, so I built one.

I took a single backend and exposed it twice, once as a stateless MCP server and once as a plain REST API, handed both to the same agent with the same tasks, and recorded what changed across 180 runs. I'm surprised that the result is less dramatic than the slogan and actually more useful: on a small tool surface the two are a tie, and on a realistic one they diverge for one structural reason each.

I'm not here to tell you "which protocol is better". But I will tell you that these two carry the **same information in different shapes**. MCP puts the tool surface in front of the model as typed schemas. REST puts it there as a contract in prose, then leans on a single generic HTTP call. Both go out on every turn, so the difference is how many tokens each one spends saying the same thing, and it is measurable.

I'm giving you the data, the harness, and a way to make a decision based on your case, not your mood.

## The experiment

I wanted any difference I measured to be the shape of the contract instead of the business logic. There is exactly one backend, a classic demo: a small store with products, inventory, orders and customers, that answers the same way every run.

Two interfaces wrap that same backend over the same six operations:

- **MCP** is modeled as native tool use on [Amazon Bedrock's Converse API](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/conversation-inference.html), because this is exactly the stateless MCP shape: the model receives tool names and JSON schemas every turn and emits a `toolUse` block that the host dispatches
- **REST** gives the model one tool, `http_request`, plus an OpenAPI-style contract in the system prompt. The model constructs the path itself. This interface also implements a real `ETag` and `304 Not Modified` cache, because conditional reads are the one thing REST can express that MCP tool use currently cannot

I gave both the same set of tasks: a simple lookup, a two-hop (order to customer name), an aggregate across a customer's orders, a missing-information recovery (an order that does not exist), a conditional (can I order an out-of-stock item?), and a repeated read that I use to test caching.

The setup:

- Model: Claude Haiku 4.5 on Amazon Bedrock, `eu-central-1`, temperature 0. I picked this small, fast model because it keeps the sandbox cost down, and a smaller model is the harder test: it is quicker to fumble a schema or burn tokens, so a difference between the two interfaces shows up instead of being hidden by a frontier model's reasoning
- Five trials per task per interface, so thirty runs each per condition
- Metrics per run: success, input and output tokens, latency, round-trips, tool calls, cache hits. A round-trip here is one model turn, so a task that makes a single tool call and then answers counts as two

## Result 1: on a small surface, it is a tie

With six tools, the internet slogan seems to be correct!

*Six tools, five trials per task, thirty runs per interface.*

| Metric | MCP | REST |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Success rate | 100% | 100% |
| Avg total tokens | 2,838 | 2,867 |
| Avg input tokens | 2,705 | 2,692 |
| Median latency | 2,116 ms | 2,070 ms |
| Avg round-trips | 2.5 | 2.5 |
| Cache hits (304) | 0 | 5 |

You can see we have the same correctness, number of round-trips, token counts and latency. If you have a handful of tools, the choice between a small MCP server and a small REST contract is just a matter of taste, not efficiency. But look at that `Cache hits` column...I'll come back to it.

## Result 2: the schema tax is real, and it scales

Then I changed the one thing I figured was about to matter: the API surface size. I ran the whole suite again with twenty-four extra endpoints, modeling a realistic store API with roughly thirty operations. On the MCP side those are *twenty-four more tool schemas*. On the REST side they are *twenty-four more lines in the contract*.

Let's see how that changed our bill:

*Thirty tools, five trials per task, thirty runs per interface.*

| Metric | MCP | REST | Delta |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Success rate | 100% | 100% | tie |
| Avg total tokens | 6,558 | 4,231 | **MCP +35%** |
| Avg input tokens | 6,406 | 4,038 | **MCP +37%** |
| Median latency | 1,996 ms | 1,810 ms | MCP +9% |
| Avg round-trips | 2.67 | 2.67 | tie |

Again, same success rate and same round-trips, but **35% more tokens**. The reason is simple: a stateless MCP server re-sends every tool schema on every turn, so the model pays for the full catalog every time, even if it doesn't use every tool. REST re-sends its contract every turn too, but a one-line contract entry costs about a third of a JSON tool schema, so it grows much more slowly.

Per task, the gap is remarkable:

| Task | MCP input tokens | REST input tokens | MCP overhead |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| order_status | 4,673 | 2,850 | +1,823 |
| customer_total | 4,732 | 2,910 | +1,822 |
| missing_order | 4,647 | 2,805 | +1,842 |
| order_customer | 7,181 | 4,500 | +2,681 |
| repeat_read | 7,318 | 4,687 | +2,631 |
| stock_mech | 9,884 | 6,475 | +3,409 |

Roughly 1,800 extra input tokens for a one-call task, and more for multi-call tasks, because the schema tax is paid **once per round-trip**. The more the agent has to go back to the tools, the more times it re-reads the whole catalog.

To be fair, this is the worst case for MCP and the best case for REST. Prompt caching on the provider side, and filtering the tool list down to what a task plausibly needs, both cut this cost. But neither is free and neither is automatic, and the structural fact remains that MCP's token cost grows with surface size about three times faster than a terse REST contract's does.

This is my measurement, so I invite you to test on your own setup and challenge my findings.

## Result 3: where REST wins outright

The `repeat_read` task asks the agent to read an order, report the total, then read it again to confirm it is unchanged. This is deliberate, to test caching.

The REST agent read the order, got an `ETag`, and on the second read sent `If-None-Match` with that tag. The server answered `304 Not Modified` with an empty body, and the agent reused the value it already had. Five cache hits in five trials. The MCP agent could not do this, because MCP tool use has no standard notion of a conditional read or a revalidation header. It called the tool again and paid for the full result a second time. No cache, baby!

The boring and old HTTP protocol with its caching mechanisms, conditional requests and revalidation, easily beats the shiny new MCP protocol on re-reads, because when your agent calls a tool it always starts from scratch, even when reading multiple times data that rarely changes.

## Result 4: where MCP wins outright

So far everything seems to be in favour of REST. I tried to build a scenario that should favour MCP.

Picture a strict, unfamiliar API. A reporting endpoint whose region codes are `EUR`, `NAM` and `APC`, not `EU` or `Europe` or `EMEA`. Metric names you cannot guess from a description. A date format that must be exactly `YYYY-MM-DD`. The kind of API an agent meets for the first time.

MCP gives the model its normal typed tool schema: the enum values are correctly spelled, the format is declared, and the host validates the call before it is dispatched. REST gets what people actually write for a terse API: a contract that names the endpoint and the parameters but does not enumerate every valid value. The agent has to infer them. I asked both, in plain language, questions like "what was net revenue in Europe on 2026-10-20?"

*Strict API, one operation, six trials per task, thirty runs per interface.*

| Metric | MCP | REST (terse contract) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Final success | 100% | 100% |
| **First-call success** | **100%** | **0%** |
| Malformed calls | 0 | 30 (one per task) |
| Avg tool calls | 1.0 | 2.0 |
| Avg round-trips | 2.0 | 3.0 |
| Avg total tokens | 1,841 | 3,041 (**+65%**) |
| Median latency | 1,720 ms | 3,006 ms (**+75%**) |

Both get there in the end, so this is not about MCP being "more correct." It is about getting it right the first time. The MCP agent mapped "Europe" to `EUR` on the first call, every single run, because the schema told it the allowed values up front. The REST agent guessed `EU` or `Europe`, got a `400`, read the error, and fixed it on the second call, every single run. That self-correction is impressive, but it costs an extra round-trip, 65% more tokens and nearly double the latency, every time.

To be honest, I could make REST match MCP by pasting the full JSON schema, enums and all, into the contract. But that is exactly the per-turn token tax that made MCP lose Result 2. The schema has to live somewhere. MCP puts it in front of the model and pays for it every turn. A terse REST contract saves those tokens right up until the API is strict enough that the saving turns into a wrong guess. No free lunch, only a choice about where you spend.

## Update: the control run

After the post went out, [izgorodin](https://dev.to/izgorodin/comment/3jfi4) read my results files more carefully than I did! The REST arm's input tokens ***grow with every turn***, so the contract is not read once. Converse is stateless, my harness doesn't use prompt caching, and the system prompt goes out on every call exactly like the tool config. Both interfaces ***pay for their description on every turn***.

So where does the 35% come from? izgorodin proposed the experiment that answers it: give REST the same thirty JSON schemas MCP gets, pasted into its contract. If its tokens land next to MCP, the gap is about the *format* of the description, not the *protocol*.

I added that third arm and ran all three in the same session: 180 more runs, 100% success everywhere.

*Average input tokens per run, five trials per task, thirty runs per arm.*

| Surface | MCP | REST (terse) | REST (with schemas) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6 tools | 2,705 | 2,692 | 3,550 |
| 30 tools | 6,406 | 4,038 | 7,542 |

The cleaner number is what the extra operations cost on every model call. Going from six to thirty operations adds:

| Arm | Extra input tokens per call |
| --- | --- |
| REST (terse contract lines) | +422 |
| MCP (tool schemas) | +1,307 |
| REST (same schemas in the contract) | +1,384 |

Same schemas, same cost. REST is even slightly more expensive, because its contract also carries the paths and the HTTP notes. Round-trips are identical, and both REST arms still get their five `304`s.

So the schema tax is real, and any interface pays it: it's the price of a dense description, charged on every turn. A JSON schema costs about three times a one-line contract entry, and that ratio is the whole 35%. It also turns Result 2 and Result 4 into one knob: how many tokens you spend describing your API on every call, and what you get back for them. A terse contract buys you cheap turns and wrong first guesses. A typed schema buys you first-call success at three times the price.

## What this does not measure

A benchmark you cannot poke holes in is a benchmark that is lying! Here are mine.

This is a very controlled scenario. One model, one small domain, six tasks. There is no authentication, no streaming, no *human in the loop*. The "wire bytes" I counted are a proxy, not a packet capture. Latency differences stayed inside the noise and were dominated by the model, not the protocol, so do not read the 9% as a protocol verdict.

And to be very clear, this measures per-request efficiency, which is not why most people reach for MCP. MCP's actual value is the ecosystem. Write one server and any agent can use it, without a previous knowledge of the contract. That portability is real and this harness does not price it. REST's hidden cost is the opposite: every consumer writes and maintains its own client, based on a shared contract.

Efficiency is one axis, but it's not the only one.

There is also a safety axis, which this harness does not touch: a stateless, per-request boundary is easier to reason about than a long-lived session, with authorization checked per call and no sticky server-side state to ride. That deserves its own measurement, so I'm thinking of a follow-up here.

## How to decide

Is stateless MCP just REST with extra steps? No.

It is REST with no cache, but with a typed, self-describing discovery layer bolted on top. Batteries included. Which one you want depends on your specific scenario:

- **Small, stable, portable tool set** that you want many agents to reuse: MCP wins. The schema tax is small and the ecosystem payoff is real.
- **Strict or unfamiliar API** with non-obvious parameters: MCP wins again. Typed, validated discovery means the agent calls correctly on the first try instead of guessing, failing, and retrying.
- **Large, loose API with cache-heavy reads and a single consumer**: a cache-friendly REST contract is the better developer experience. You avoid the schema tax and you get `304`s for free.
- **Somewhere in between**: measure it. That is the whole point of the harness.

There is no winner-take-all. It is a trade-off about how much you spend describing your API, and what you get back for it, and now I hope it is a trade-off you can put some numbers on.

## Run it yourself

The full harness is on GitHub: [mcp-vs-rest-bench](https://github.com/edodusi/mcp-vs-rest-bench). The backend, the two interfaces, the task suite, the runner, and the raw results JSON. It runs against Amazon Bedrock on demand, so there is nothing to tear down, no standing infrastructure, and a full five-trial sweep costs a few cents of Haiku tokens. Point it at your own stack, your own tasks, your own model, and settle your own version of the argument.

Don't decide with vibes. Decide with data.

---

# “Error while dexing”: how an Android build failure led me to a dying SSD
URL: https://edoardodusi.com/blog/2026/error-while-dexing.html
Date: 2026-07-30
Reading time: 8 min

A dying disk doesn't announce itself like Roy Batty, with tears in rain. It sneaks in wearing a mask: the face of the first thing that happens to touch a bad sector.

Mine looked like a Gradle bug. Claude Code saw through the disguise almost immediately. I didn't believe it at first, so I made it walk me through the evidence.

## From a dexing error to an I/O error

The release build of CodeRoutine failed every time on the same dependency:

```text
Execution failed for DexingNoClasspathTransform: .../tink-android-1.8.0.jar
  > Error while dexing.
```

If you've worked on Android, that points you toward software: a dependency conflict, a D8/R8 mismatch, a stale cache or some incompatibility between the library and the toolchain.

We checked the obvious explanations first. A corrupted Gradle cache was plausible, but rebuilding it did not solve the failure. Memory pressure from orphaned Gradle daemons was plausible too, and wrong too.

Then we looked one layer lower. A debug build had produced a less friendly but much more useful message:

```text
AsmClassesTransform … > Input/output error
```

And underneath Gradle's summary, `--stacktrace` exposed the exception that mattered:

```text
java.io.IOException
```

The toolchain wasn't rejecting the jar, it couldn't read it!

A single command confirmed that Gradle was not involved:

```bash
cat ~/.gradle/caches/.../tink-android-1.8.0.jar > /dev/null
```

It returned an I/O error. After a couple of “Discombobulating…”, Claude Code was blunt: this was not a corrupted jar, this was a clear indicator of a failing drive.

That conclusion surprised me, so I asked for details and evidence. The kernel log provided both:

```text
nvme1n1: I/O Cmd(0x2) @ LBA 311368392, 256 blocks, I/O Error (sct 0x2 / sc 0x81)
critical medium error, dev nvme1n1, sector 311368392 op 0x0:(READ)
BTRFS error (device nvme1n1p3): errs: wr 0, rd 5266, flush 0, corrupt 0, gen 0
```

`sct 0x2 / sc 0x81` is an unrecovered read error: the drive itself could not return the data.

We then scanned all 1,285 artifacts in the Gradle cache for readability in one pass. Three were unreadable. I deleted them, Gradle downloaded clean copies and the build went green.

The Android problem was solved, but the problem with my computer had just started.

## SMART said PASSED

The drive was a Fanxiang S770 2TB with 943 power-on hours and 4.8 TB written. Its headline looked reassuring:

```text
SMART overall-health self-assessment test result: PASSED
```

But that was a lie. The useful information was a few lines below:

| Metric | Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Media and Data Integrity Errors | **50** | Unrecoverable data-loss events; this should be zero |
| Available Spare | **89%** | 11% of the reserve had already been consumed |
| Percentage Used | **0%** | Essentially no write wear |
| Error Information Log Entries | **27,466** | Repeated attempts against failing reads |

NVMe's overall-health result only fails when a Critical Warning bit is set, and mine was still `0x00`. The spare-capacity warning would not fire until Available Spare fell below its threshold, 25% on this drive.

So the headline said `PASSED` while the counters described a nearly new SSD with 50 unrecoverable errors and 11% of its spare pool already gone. Zero wear made ordinary ageing a poor explanation. This looked like an early-life manufacturing defect.

## Turning the failure into a rescue

At that point the priority changed. I no longer cared about **fixing** the hardware, I wanted a backup of everything that could not be regenerated.

Reading flash does not consume NAND endurance, writes do. But here I discovered that failed reads are different. The controller retries them aggressively and may relocate a marginal block, **consuming spare capacity** in the process. On this drive the expensive operation was not reading data once, it was repeatedly reading the same damaged regions.

That shaped the recovery: no separate scan followed by a backup. The *backup itself* would be the scan.

We built a one-pass process around `tar`:

```bash
tar --create --ignore-failed-read --numeric-owner --acls --xattrs \
    --directory "$HOME" -- "$folder" 2>"$log" | \
    zstd -1 -T0 -o "$dest/$folder.tar.zst"
```

`--ignore-failed-read` logs unreadable files and continues. The stderr log becomes the casualty list while the readable data goes directly to a healthy USB disk.

Verification happens against that new disk, without touching the NVMe again:

```bash
zstd -t archive.tar.zst && \
tar -tf archive.tar.zst --use-compress-program='zstd -d'
```

The recovery also forced me to *define* what was actually irreplaceable. My repositories had GitHub remotes and nothing unpushed. Build caches, Steam libraries, models and downloads could all be recreated. What mattered was much smaller: personal notes, dotfiles, keys, `.env` files and a couple of `google-services.json` files.

That is why this backup was an allow-list rather than an exclude-list. Instead of trying to describe all the disposable bulk on the disk, I named the small set of things that existed nowhere else.

When the process reached private SSH keys, cloud credentials and a GitHub token, Claude Code's permission guardrail stopped the action and handed the decision back to me. That was *absolutely right*! Disaster recovery is not a reason for an agent to move credentials onto an external device without explicit approval.

## What had happened to the SSD

With the important data safe, we could investigate the drive more aggressively.

The decisive clue was not another counter but a timestamp. One damaged Firefox cache entry had been written on 2025-09-30, ten months before it became unreadable. The write had apparently succeeded, so the data degraded in place.

SSD bad-block handling is good at catching cells that fail during a write. It is much less helpful when cells accept data and lose their charge later. That explained why Gradle had downloaded valid jars that became unreadable weeks afterwards.

Successive Btrfs scrubs showed another important pattern:

| Scrub | Read errors | Corrected | Uncorrectable | Files named |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 800 | 771 | 29 | 23 |
| 2 | 448 | 423 | 25 | 4 |
| 3 | 96 | 86 | 10 | 1 |

Each run named different files. Some files that failed once could be read on the next attempt. So it was clear that these were not simply hard-dead sectors that failed consistently, but marginal cells *failing probabilistically*.

If that sounds bad, it’s actually worse. A permanently dead sector is at least honest, a scrub finds it every time. A marginal cell can pass today's scan and fail next week, turning repeated scrubs into whack-a-mole.

Luckily, every damaged file we found belonged to Steam or Proton, a browser cache or an Android emulator image. Nothing irreplaceable was lost.

Across four scans, the hardware counters remained stable: Media Errors stayed at 50, Available Spare at 89% and Btrfs `corruption_errs` at zero. The damaged sectors were concentrated in two clusters inside the first 192 GB of the 2 TB device. The defect looked localised rather than actively spreading, but the drive had already destroyed data twice. It was no longer trustworthy as a system disk.

## Where this left the drive

I claimed the warranty. In the EU, the two-year legal guarantee of conformity is provided by the seller and is independent of the manufacturer's warranty. The drive was about twelve months old, and one conversation with the retailer produced an approved refund.

The diagnostic evidence made the case straightforward: normal temperatures, 0% wear, 50 media errors and defects concentrated in one physical region. This was not a drive worn out by heavy use.

Whether I will immediately replace it is a separate question. A comparable 2 TB SSD currently costs much more than I paid, while this one fails loudly: reads return `EIO` rather than silently producing corrupted bytes, and Btrfs reported no checksum corruption across four scans. That might make it tolerable as scratch space for Steam libraries or build caches, data that is never the only copy, but never again as the disk holding my home directory.

The lesson worth keeping has nothing to do with SMART counters or NVMe error codes. It's that, left alone, I might never have suspected the disk at all: I would still be debugging Gradle, because that is what the symptom told me to do. It took Claude Code to see how much distance a failure can put between itself and its first symptom.

An Android build said it could not dex a jar. Gradle made that look like a software problem. The stacktrace turned it into an I/O problem. The kernel turned it into an NVMe problem. It was Claude Code that followed that chain down, tested every layer and recovered the data once we reached the bottom. My job was mostly asking for evidence and approving the next step.

A failing disk wears the mask of whatever touches the bad sector first. This one happened to look like Gradle.

If I had kept using that NVMe as my primary disk, my data would have been lost in time, like tears in rain.

---

# Welcome to my new website and blog!
URL: https://edoardodusi.com/blog/2026/welcome.html
Date: 2026-07-24
Reading time: 2 min

It was about time I gave my personal website a proper refresh. Welcome to the new home for my writing, speaking engagements, and side projects!

For this iteration, I wanted to keep things blisteringly fast and extremely minimal. Instead of reaching for a heavy JavaScript framework or a complex CMS, I decided to build a custom, zero-dependency Static Site Generator (SSG). 

## Under the Hood

The entire site is served as static HTML directly from GitHub Pages. The styling uses modern, vanilla CSS with CSS Variables for seamless light and dark mode switching. 

For the blog, I wrote a tiny Node.js build script that parses markdown files and generates the static HTML. 

```javascript
// A tiny peek at our custom build script
const fm = require('front-matter');
const { marked } = require('marked');

const parsed = fm(markdownContent);
const htmlContent = marked.parse(parsed.body);
```

I even added custom syntax highlighting using **Highlight.js** (specifically the gorgeous Dracula theme) so code snippets look perfectly crisp whether you are reading in light or dark mode. 

## What's Next?

I plan to use this space to share more in-depth thoughts on web development, Developer Relations, software architecture, and the open-source ecosystem. 

Stay tuned for more updates, and feel free to reach out on my socials if you have any questions about the setup!
